name: Sulbutiamine
short: Case report: addiction to sulbutiamine disrupted a bipolar patient's care. Depression trial: safety like placebo, no mania or suicide attempts. Fewer side effects than imipramine in children.
text: Safety evidence for sulbutiamine is limited. A case report described a patient with bipolar disorder who became addicted to sulbutiamine and needed ever-increasing amounts, which severely compromised his psychiatric care; the authors warned doctors about the potential misuse of this product, which is available without prescription or over the internet. In an 8-week multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial in hospital inpatients with major depression who were also taking clomipramine, the safety data were comparable between groups, and sulbutiamine did not induce inappropriate behaviour, suicide attempts or mania; the abstract does not give the number of patients. In a randomised trial in 450 children aged 6 to 18 with bedwetting, comparing sulbutiamine, imipramine and the two together for six months with no placebo group, adverse effects were less frequent with sulbutiamine (4.7% to 6%) than with imipramine (12% to 14%); the abstract does not say what the adverse effects were. In an uncontrolled two-month study in 26 people with multiple sclerosis, there were no serious adverse events. Apart from these combinations with clomipramine and imipramine, no interaction data were found in the cited sources.
